name: Appeal to emotion
statement: Stirring feeling in place of giving a reason is called a fallacy, and emotional framing damages fallacy detection more than it improves how convincing an argument seems.
meaning: Three separate claims travel under one label, and the textbook name only covers the third. The first is that a message arouses the feeling it aims at. The second is that people exposed to it end up holding different attitudes or doing different things. The third is that the feeling stands in for a reason, so a listener accepts a claim they had no grounds to accept. Only the third is a fallacy, and it is the one least often measured. Hansen's survey of the field draws the line by use rather than by content: appeals to pity and appeals to force have their natural home in practical reasoning, where a threat or a hardship genuinely bears on what to do, and the charge of fallacy attaches when the same appeal is offered as a reason to believe something. Appraisal theories push from the other side. Moors, Ellsworth, Scherer and Frijda define appraisal as a process that detects and assesses the significance of an event for a person's concerns, which makes an emotion the output of an assessment rather than noise arriving alongside one. An emotion so produced can be information about the situation, and an argument that a listener may be right to weigh.

origin.where: Logick; or, The Right Use of Reason
origin.note: Hansen's Stanford Encyclopedia survey records that Watts extended Locke's four ad-arguments with three more, among them argumentum ad passiones, and that Watts treated these as kinds of argument rather than as fallacies. The fallacy reading is later. The same survey places ad baculum, ad misericordiam and ad populum in the class of fallacies of relevance in Copi's Introduction to Logic, cited there as 1961, and describes that class as exploiting psychological rather than logical associations. Watts and Copi were not read here.

evidence: The largest measurement is of persuasion rather than of fallacy. Tannenbaum and colleagues meta-analysed fear appeals across 127 articles, 9% of them unpublished, yielding 248 independent samples and 27,372 participants. The average random-effects effect on a composite of attitudes, intentions and behaviours was d = 0.29, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.35, with heterogeneity Q(247) = 1,287 and I-squared of 85.11. In the 71 samples carrying a manipulation check, treatment groups reported more fear than comparison groups at d = 1.00, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.18. Four moderators separated: messages including efficacy statements gave 0.43, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.55 across 92 samples against 0.21, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.29 across 154 without; one-time recommended behaviours gave 0.43, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.56 against 0.21, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.29 for repeated ones; messages high on both depicted susceptibility and severity gave 0.39, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.50 against 0.12, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.27 for messages high on neither; and a metaregression on the percentage of the sample that was female gave b = 0.0031, SE 0.0012, 95% CI 0.0007 to 0.0055. Comparing moderate with high depicted fear gave d = -0.05, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.24, across 21 samples, so more fear past a point bought nothing and cost nothing. The authors report no level of any moderator at which fear appeals backfired. Whether ordinary arguers treat emotional appeals as unreasonable was tested by van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels across a research programme summarised in a single table, on a seven-point scale where 1 is very unreasonable, 4 neither and 7 very reasonable. The argumentum ad misericordiam scored 3.86 against 5.06 for its non-fallacious counterpart. The argumentum ad baculum scored 2.04 in its physical variant, 2.91 non-physical, 1.86 direct and 3.72 indirect, against counterparts of 5.64 and 5.41. The argumentum ad populum scored 2.77 against 5.88. Whether emotion damages the evaluation of an argument is a third literature. Blanchette and Richards gave participants conditional statements and varied the emotionality of the terms, using pre-existing emotional words in one experiment and words made emotional by classical conditioning in the other, and found more invalid inferences drawn from emotional statements in both. Chen and colleagues ran the nearest thing to a direct test of the fallacy claim. They used large language models to inject emotional appeals into fallacious arguments while holding the premise and conclusion structure fixed, building 1,000 arguments, 200 of them originals, and had each of 20 batches rated by the same three recruits from Prolific. The share of arguments people labelled fallacious fell from about 91% to about 86%, a relative drop of 5.5%, and macro F1 for naming the fallacy type fell from 0.563 on the originals to a model average of 0.473, a relative drop of about 14.5%. Convincingness moved by 0.04 of a standard deviation. Mean convincingness was 1.67 on a five-point scale, with 59.1% of ratings at the floor.

replication.headline: Emotional content changes how people evaluate an argument in study after study, and whether it degrades accuracy or improves it turns on whether the emotion is relevant to what is being argued about.
replication.detail: Blanchette and Richards found more invalid inferences on emotional material in two experiments in 2004. Blanchette, Richards, Melnyk and Lavda tested people in London, Manchester and London, Ontario within a week of the July 2005 attacks and again six months later, using neutral, generally emotional and terrorism-related syllogisms. Participants overall reasoned more accurately on the neutral problems, and the London participants gave more logically valid answers on the terrorism problems, and were less likely to answer from belief, while reporting higher levels of emotion. Blanchette, Gavigan and Johnston set out to reconcile the two results across four experiments, separating integral emotion, evoked by the content being reasoned about, from incidental emotion evoked by images or videos unrelated to it. Emotion lowered the proportion of normatively correct responses only in the irrelevant condition; in the relevant condition it produced no reliable deleterious effect. The persuasion side of the claim is contested in a different way. Kok, Peters, Kessels, ten Hoor and Ruiter reviewed the same literature Tannenbaum pooled and concluded that it does not support positive effects of fear appeals, arguing that a sound test must compare a threatening with a non-threatening intervention under both high and low efficacy and must measure behaviour. Health Psychology Review published seven commentaries on that paper and a rejoinder from its authors.

study.cite: Blanchette, I., Gavigan, S., & Johnston, K. (2014). Does emotion help or hinder reasoning? The moderating role of relevance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(3), 1049-1064.

limits: Fear appeal research measures persuasion, not fallaciousness. Tannenbaum's pooled 0.29 says that people exposed to frightening messages ended up closer to the advocated position; it says nothing about whether any of them accepted a claim on grounds that were not reasons. No entry in that meta-analysis was designed to answer that question. The pooled figure is also disputed. Tannenbaum's own introduction records that earlier meta-analyses disagreed, naming Witte and Allen in 2000 as positive, de Hoog and colleagues in 2007 as null and Peters and colleagues in 2013 as negative; none of those three was read here. Kok and colleagues were read only as the PubMed abstract, the Taylor and Francis full text being unavailable through the routes tried. The three Blanchette papers are paywalled and were also read only as PubMed abstracts, so this entry carries their directions and their designs and none of their numbers. The van Eemeren figures come from van Eemeren and Garssen's summary table of a programme running over more than ten years, not from the individual experiments, which were not obtained; that table prints means with no measure of spread and does not give sample sizes. Chen and colleagues is a preprint. Its stimuli were written by language models, its raters were crowdworkers judging a five-way fallacy scheme, and agreement on the emotion labels was poor, with Cohen's kappa between -0.005 and 0.139 against 0.014 to 0.591 for the fallacy labels. Searches at Crossref, Europe PMC and general web search, pairing appeal-to-emotion, ad misericordiam and pathos with meta-analysis and replication terms, turned up no meta-analysis of the fallacy itself and no fear appeal meta-analysis later than Tannenbaum's.
misreadings: Calling something a fallacy is not a claim that it fails to work, and here the two readings point in opposite directions. Fear appeals were effective at every level of every moderator Tannenbaum tested, and the paper reports no condition in which they backfired. Neither is attitude change evidence that a bad argument was accepted, which is the trap this whole area sets. Chen's emotionally framed arguments were rated 0.04 of a standard deviation more convincing while detection of their flaws fell by about 14.5%, and arguments people did label fallacious were rated less convincing than those they did not. The label also flattens a graded thing. On van Eemeren's scale a direct threat sat at 1.86 and an appeal to pity at 3.86, close to the midpoint marked neither reasonable nor unreasonable, so ordinary arguers are already distinguishing cases the textbook lists together. Emotion is not irrelevant by definition either. Hansen's survey locates appeals to pity and to force in practical reasoning, where they bear on what to do, and places the fallacy in their doxastic use. Appraisal theories make the stronger version of the point, treating an emotion as the product of a process that assesses an event's significance for the person's concerns. Two neighbouring entries are about different claims. The affect heuristic concerns feelings standing in for risk and probability judgements, and one of its predictions failed across 7,218 people in Many Labs 2. Emotional reasoning runs from a person's own anxiety to a belief that the world is dangerous, which is an inference about a situation rather than a move in an argument.
